# Introduction

In the main `02_estimation_methods.R` script, we implemented **"White-Box"** code. This means we manually defined the underlying mathematics (like explicitly writing the log-likelihood functions, algebra for Bergman Weights, and root-finding for Moments). We did this to create an authentic educational pipeline where students can see exactly *how* the algorithms arrive at their parameters.

However, in a production environment where you just want results quickly, R provides **"Black-Box"** functions. These are optimized, robust, one-liner functions embedded in standard packages that solve the same problems instantly. 

This document contrasts the verbosity of our educational code against the brevity of production-ready packages.

---

# 1. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

MLE is the industry standard for estimating Weibull parameters with right-censored data.

### The Detailed "White-Box" Approach
In our code, we explicitly mapped the failure likelihoods against the censored survival probabilities, resulting in an ~30-line custom implementation passed to a general-purpose optimizer (`optim`):

```{r}
# Manual Log-Likelihood & Nelder-Mead Optimization (~30 Lines)
neg_loglik <- function(log_params) {
  k   <- exp(log_params[1])
  lam <- exp(log_params[2])
  
  t_ratio <- t / lam
  
  # Log-PDF for failures
  ll_fail <- sum(event * (log(k) - log(lam) + (k - 1) * log(t_ratio) - t_ratio^k))
  # Log-survival for censored
  ll_cens <- sum((1 - event) * (-t_ratio^k))
  
  return(-(ll_fail + ll_cens))
}

result <- optim(par = c(log(1.5), log(mean_t)), 
                fn = neg_loglik, 
                method = "Nelder-Mead")

k_hat   <- exp(result$par[1])
lam_hat <- exp(result$par[2])
```

### The "Black-Box" One-Liner
In production, you would never write your own likelihood function. You would use the `survival` package, which is arguably the most battle-tested survival analysis library in existence. 

```{r}
# Using the survival package (1 Line)
library(survival)

fit <- survreg(Surv(lifetime_days, failed) ~ 1, data = drive_data, dist = "weibull")

# Note: survreg uses the "Extreme Value" parameterization. 
# To convert to standard Weibull shape/scale:
k_hat   <- 1 / fit$scale
lam_hat <- exp(coef(fit))
```

*Code Reduction:* **30 lines** down to **1 line**.

---

# 2. OLS / Median Rank Regression (MRR)

OLS fits a linear regression line to coordinate transformations of the empirical failures.

### The Detailed "White-Box" Approach
We manually calculated Benard's median ranks, transformed the axes to the Weibull scale, and explicitly applied R's `lm()` function:

```{r}
# Manual Rank Transformation (~15 lines)
t_fail <- sort(drive_data$lifetime_days[drive_data$failed == 1])
n <- length(t_fail)

# Benard's formula
i <- seq_len(n)
F_i <- (i - 0.3) / (n + 0.4)

# Linearization
Y <- log(-log(1 - F_i)) 
X <- log(t_fail)

fit <- lm(Y ~ X)
k_hat   <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
lam_hat <- exp(-unname(coef(fit)[1]) / k_hat)
```

### The "Black-Box" One-Liner
If you need Rank Regression in R, the specialized `WeibullR` package handles all of this automatically, converting and plotting in one swift move.

```{r}
# Using WeibullR (1 Line)
library(WeibullR)

fit <- wblr.fit(wblr(t_fail), method.fit = "rr")
```

*Code Reduction:* **15 lines** down to **1 line**.

---

# 3. Kaplan-Meier Survival Benchmark

The Kaplan-Meier estimator is exactly what we just added to the lecture documents to prove why MLE works better than WLS for censored drives.

### The Detailed "White-Box" Approach
Plotting this manually requires grouping data, keeping track of the risk set at each time step $t$, calculating running survival probabilities $\prod (1 - d_i/n_i)$, and building a step-function graph. If coded sequentially, it easily takes **20-40 lines**.

### The "Black-Box" One-Liner
The `survival` package calculates this using the formula instantly.

```{r}
# Using survival and broom for instant calculation (~2 Lines)
library(survival)

km_fit <- survfit(Surv(lifetime_days, failed) ~ 1, data = drive_data)
# Plotting is as easy as:
plot(km_fit, conf.int = TRUE, mark.time = TRUE)
```

---

# Conclusion

While the **White-Box** code makes our project significantly longer, it acts as a digital textbook. It strips away the magic of libraries like `survival` and `WeibullR` to reveal exactly how statistical mathematics translates to code. 

When you move into actual corporate analytics, you will discard the detailed scripts found in `02_estimation_methods.R` and instead pipeline everything through the **Black-Box** one-liners shown above!
